notes.meaning: Nehemiah the governor and Zedekiah put their seals onto the written covenant to obey God. Nehemiah signed first because he was the royal governor sent by the king of Persia. Zedekiah was most likely his chief secretary or another leading ruler. Putting their official seals on the document showed that their commitment was serious and binding.

The priests signed next, led by Seraiah, Azariah, and Jeremiah. Most of these names represent high-ranking priestly family lines rather than single individuals. These families were pledging to lead the worship of God faithfully.

More priestly family leaders added their seals to the document. These men were responsible for carrying out the sacrifices and teaching God's commands to the nation. By signing, they bound all the priests under their care to follow the law.

The list of priests finishes with these final names, making twenty-one priestly families in all. They officially committed themselves to keep temple worship pure and active. Their example showed the whole nation that spiritual leaders must walk with God first.

The Levites signed after the priests, beginning with Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel. These were the very men who had just helped lead the people in public prayer and Bible teaching. Now they took the lead in making a binding promise to obey what they had taught.

This list completes the seventeen Levite leaders who set their seals to the covenant. The Levites assisted the priests, cared for the temple, and led the music. Their shared signatures showed complete unity in wanting to obey God.

The civic and community leaders signed next, starting with Parosh, Pahath-moab, and Elam. It was impossible for every citizen in the country to seal the scroll personally. Therefore, these family chiefs signed on behalf of all the people they represented.

More clan heads and town leaders stepped forward to seal the written agreement. Many of these names were connected to towns where returning families had settled. Their presence showed that obedience was expected in every village, not just inside Jerusalem.

The roll of family heads continues through these verses. These men directed everyday affairs and settled disagreements among their neighbors. By signing, they promised to manage their communities according to God's standards.

Another group of civic elders added their names to the growing list of signers. These leaders were willing to be held publicly accountable before God and their neighbors. Their public stand encouraged the rest of the community to remain faithful.

The list of the forty-four community leaders ends with these names. In all, eighty-four officials, priests, and Levites sealed the covenant on behalf of Israel. The document now carried the full authority of the returned nation's leadership.

The rest of the people gave their full consent even though they could not sign the scroll. This included temple singers, gatekeepers, helpers, and former foreigners who had turned away from idols to serve God. Wives and children old enough to understand also joined in the agreement.

The whole company united with their leaders and bound themselves with an oath and a curse. Taking a curse meant asking God to bring His discipline upon them if they broke their word. Rich and poor stood together as brothers, promising to obey all the commandments God had given through Moses.

The people made a specific promise not to let their sons and daughters marry people from pagan nations. In the past, marrying idol worshippers had dragged Israel into worshiping false gods. They pledged to protect the purity of their families and remain loyal to the Lord.

The people promised not to buy goods or food on the Sabbath or on any holy festival day. They also resolved to leave their fields unfarmed every seventh year and to cancel debts at that time. Observing these days proved they trusted God to provide for their needs without breaking His holy rest.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that this verse combines rules from different parts of the Pentateuch, showing that the post-exilic community possessed and honored the complete books of Moses.

notes.meaning: The community set up an annual tax of a third of a shekel to keep the temple running. God's ancient law had asked for half a shekel in certain census seasons, but the widespread poverty of the returned exiles made this smaller yearly sum practical. This contribution gave the house of God a regular income for its daily work.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that a third of a Persian shekel equaled the silver weight of the older Hebrew half-shekel, or that the Exodus rule was a census tax rather than an annual fee.

notes.meaning: The temple tax paid for the holy bread on the table, the daily morning and evening sacrifices, and the special offerings on Sabbaths and feasts. It also funded the sin offerings that provided atonement, which means the sacrifice that restored peace between God and His people. Everyone shared in the cost so that worship would never stop.

The priests, Levites, and people cast lots to decide when each family clan had to bring firewood to the temple. The fire on God's altar had to burn day and night, so it required a constant supply of wood. Casting lots gave each group an orderly and fair schedule to provide for the altar.

The people bound themselves to bring the very first part of their farm crops and fruit harvests to the Lord's house each year. Under the Law of Moses, offering the first harvest showed gratitude and faith that God would supply the rest. Bringing these gifts ensured that the priests had fresh food while serving at the temple.

Parents pledged to redeem their firstborn sons and unclean animals by paying a set price to the priests, as the law commanded. Meanwhile, the firstborn of clean animals like sheep and cattle were brought straight to the altar as offerings. This practice reminded the people that every life belongs to God, who had rescued them from slavery.

The people promised to bring bread dough, grain, wine, and olive oil to the temple storehouses for the priests. They also agreed to pay a tithe, meaning a tenth of all their field crops, to the Levites in their home towns. Because the Levites had no farm fields of their own, these tithes were their only source of food.

differ.view: Giving a tenth of one's income remains a binding command for Christians today to support the work of the church.
Tithing was part of the Old Testament law for Israel, so Christians are called to give generously and cheerfully without a required percentage.

notes.meaning: A priest from Aaron's family was ordered to be present whenever the Levites collected the tithes out in the farming towns. After receiving the people's gifts, the Levites brought a tenth of those tithes to the temple treasury in Jerusalem for the priests. Having a priest supervise the collection prevented dishonesty and made sure everyone gave the correct share.

The people and Levites promised to bring their contributions of grain, wine, and oil right to the temple rooms where the sacred vessels were stored. These provisions supported the priests, temple guards, and singers who served on duty. They concluded their solemn covenant by declaring they would never neglect the house of their God.
